items.title: Assessing User-Subjective Experience with Conversational Agents for Behavioral and Mental Health Interventions: Design and Psychometric Evaluation of CUE-Chat
items.abstract: While AI-conversational agents are increasingly integrated into behavioral and mental health interventions, standardized instruments to assess their performance remain scarce. To address this gap, we developed an instrument to measure user-subjective experience with AI-driven agents in the healthcare domain. We focused on user perception due to its direct contribution to intervention effects, and on healthcare given that the rapid adoption of AI-agents in this domain continues to outpace the development of validated evaluation instruments. Across four studies, we developed and tested the Chatbot User Evaluation instrument (CUE-Chat). First, we identified relevant assessment domains and items through literature review, existing instruments, input from AI-driven agents, and the research team’s domain expertise. Following this, we requested feedback on draft subscales, definitions, and items from expert and laypeople panels. We then tested the structure of the instrument’s concept version. Finally, we conducted a psychometric evaluation and finalized the instrument.CUE-Chat consists of four factors: Perceived Efficacy (4 items), Usability (4 items), Intelligence (4 items), and Safety and Risk Management (4 items). Reliability and validity of the total score and each subscale was good to excellent (Cronbach’s α = .73-.92; Ω = .74-.93). Predictive validity was strong with all scales predictive of users’ overall rating of an AI-agent’s performance.We conclude that CUE-Chat’s strong psychometric properties are promising, and that it is particularly useful for researchers integrating AI-driven agents into behavioral and mental health interventions in both developmental and evaluative stages.

items.title: Authentic assessment in an AI-integrated qualitative research methods course
items.abstract: Abstract Authentic assessment has been a recognized aspiration in higher education for nearly four decades, yet its implementation at the undergraduate level has remained constrained by the procedural demands of professional-level work. Generative artificial intelligence reshapes the implementation calculus by lowering the entry barriers that previously confined authentic assessment to capstone courses, professional programs, and elite institutional contexts. This paper presents a single-semester case study of an AI-integrated qualitative research methods course taught to undergraduates in a child and adolescent development program at a regional public university. Twenty-one students used a custom AI class companion without restriction to produce full-length qualitative research manuscripts. The analytic backbone is a five-dimensional model of authentic assessment, with its physical-context dimension extended to require AI inclusion in fields where professional practice now incorporates the technology. Three rubric-proximal proxy indicators were estimated across the corpus: methods specificity, claim-evidence coupling, and theory-interpretation linkage density. The methods specificity proxy compresses toward the upper bound of its scale, indicating that AI scaffolding supports structural elements of qualitative writing effectively. The two judgment-dependent proxies retain wide dispersion. Process tracing of four contrasting cases identifies three pathways that distinguish stronger from weaker outcomes: criteria-based orchestration, irreducible input supply, and substantive iteration. The boundary-condition pattern indicates that authentic assessment in AI-integrated courses remains diagnostic where it needs to be and is supported where it needed support.

items.title: Dari mesin jawaban menjadi teman berpikir: Reorientasi peran artificial intelligence dalam pembelajaran mendalam di pendidikan tinggi
items.abstract: Perkembangan generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) telah mengubah cara mahasiswa memperoleh, mengolah, dan menghasilkan pengetahuan di pendidikan tinggi. Kemudahan memperoleh jawaban secara instan meningkatkan efisiensi pembelajaran, tetapi juga berpotensi mendorong cognitive offloading dan mengurangi keterlibatan mahasiswa dalam proses berpikir. Artikel ini bertujuan menganalisis pembelajaran mendalam (deep learning pedagogy) sebagai respons pedagogis terhadap disrupsi GenAI serta merumuskan reorientasi peran AI dari answer machine menjadi thinking partner. Penelitian menggunakan pendekatan kualitatif dengan desain analisis konseptual melalui sintesis literatur ilmiah, teori, dan dokumen kebijakan mengenai GenAI, cognitive offloading, konstruktivisme, berpikir kritis, metakognisi, dan pembelajaran mendalam. Hasil sintesis menunjukkan bahwa persoalan utama penggunaan GenAI bukan keberadaan cognitive offloading, melainkan pendelegasian aktivitas kognitif yang menggantikan proses berpikir yang menjadi tujuan pembelajaran. Artikel ini merumuskan efficiency–depth paradox, yaitu ketegangan antara peningkatan efisiensi melalui AI dan kebutuhan untuk mempertahankan kedalaman proses belajar. Pembelajaran mendalam melalui prinsip mindful, meaningful, dan joyful learning dapat berfungsi sebagai pedagogical safeguards. Reorientasi AI sebagai thinking partner menempatkan mahasiswa sebagai primary thinker, sementara AI berfungsi sebagai scaffolding untuk questioning, exploration, feedback, verification, dan reflection.

items.title: Decision Theory and Artificial Intelligence: An Anatomical Review of Output Contracts, Acquisition Geometries, and Epistemic Verticals
items.abstract: This paper presents a detailed anatomical review of Miquel Noguer i Alonso's "Decision Theory and Artificial Intelligence" (2026). The reviewed work develops a unified Bayesian decision-theoretic framework that links feasible action spaces, reward functions, statistical estimation targets, and costly information acquisition policies. Central contributions include minimal output contracts for specified reward families (Theorem 4.5), regret propagation decompositions (Proposition 6.1), capacity-constrained optimal gates with complementary slackness (Theorem 7.1), an acquisition-output contract characterising compressed representations that preserve nonnegative-price routing decisions (Theorem 7.6), and a routing-geometry dichotomy between discrete decisions (information most valuable near action boundaries) and continuous quadratic sizing (precision gains favouring strongest signals) (Proposition 7.13). The framework accommodates supervised, unsupervised, and reinforcement learning, large language models, and typed probability interfaces such as JEV. A retrospective empirical study of 27,241 LLM cases evaluates cost-aware replacement routing. This review systematically examines the paper's strengths and limitations, situates it against at least ten competing models and theories in decision theory, statistical treatment rules, cascade deferral, metareasoning, and decision-focused learning, and articulates the ontological and epistemological verticals underlying the evolution of its central themes. Possible extensions and ideation pathways are proposed. All references follow Harvard style. KSCCN review article, 11 October 2026. Dr. Syed Muntasir Mamun, ORCID 0000-0001-6845-2853. The views expressed are those of the author.

items.title: Delegation Is Not Assistance: Agentic AI and Assessment Governance in Higher Education - A Comparative Documentary Analysis of 12 Universities
items.abstract: Generative AI (GenAI) assessment policies in higher education have centred on originality, disclosure, and permission to use AI. Agentic AI, which can plan, use tools, access platforms, and act with limited human intervention, challenges this logic because it can take over the whole action chain of an assessed task rather than only generate content. This study examines how assessment governance changes from GenAI to agentic AI. Using exploratory comparative documentary analysis, public central guidance from 12 universities was theoretically sampled: six agentic-aware cases and six GenAI-dominant comparators, with a retrieval cut-off of 3 October 2026. Documents were coded on six dimensions using a directed framework informed by Bacchi’s “What’s the Problem Represented to Be?” approach. All agentic-aware cases distinguished agentic AI from GenAI, and most set explicit delegation and access boundaries, whereas no comparator explicitly addressed agents operating institutional systems on a student’s behalf. The comparators, however, were strong on evidence of learning and task-level transparency, and programme-level assurance was sparse in both groups. The study proposes the Delegation-Evidence-Access (DEA) framework, which moves governance from tool permission towards responsibility allocation, and derives four assessment contexts and a task-, course-, and programme-level implementation model. Implications for Malaysian higher education are discussed. Findings are descriptive, based on selected public documents, and not representative; no inter-rater reliability was assessed.

items.title: Effects of AI-Supported Learning on Independent Cognitive Performance: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of Instructional Scaffolding and Learner Characteristics
items.abstract: This systematic review and meta-analysis will examine the effects of AI-supported learning on objectively assessed cognitive performance when AI assistance is unavailable during assessment. It will cover intelligent tutoring systems, traditional chatbots, adaptive learning platforms, and generative AI across educational stages and subject areas. Technology characteristics and instructional support functions will be coded separately, allowing overlapping features rather than imposing mutually exclusive technology categories. The primary objective is to estimate the effects of AI-supported learning compared with non-AI learning conditions on independent cognitive performance. Secondary objectives are to examine direct comparisons between AI-supported instructional approaches and whether effects vary with baseline learner characteristics and instructional support functions. Relevant support functions include hints, explanations, feedback, worked examples, self-explanation prompts, verification and revision prompts, adaptive learning pathways, and restrictions or fading of AI assistance. Randomized and non-randomized controlled intervention studies will be synthesized separately. A distinct observational evidence stream will examine associations between actual AI use, such as usage frequency, help-seeking, and verification behaviors, and eligible cognitive outcomes. These associations will not be combined with intervention effects or interpreted as causal evidence that a particular use behavior improves learning. Eligible outcomes include objective measures of knowledge and understanding, application and transfer, other cognitive skills, and composite achievement, which will be analyzed separately. The first eligible post-intervention assessment and subsequent delayed assessments will be distinguished. Assessments must be completed without AI; access to non-AI resources will be recorded separately. Unclear AI permissions will remain awaiting clarification rather than being treated as confirmed eligibility or grounds for automatic exclusion. Two human reviewers will independently screen records, extract key study information, and assess risk of bias, with disagreements reconciled. Analyses will account for overlapping reports, shared samples, dependent effect sizes, and differences in study design and comparison conditions. Moderator analyses will depend on sufficient comparable evidence. Within-study learner moderation will be distinguished from between-study associations. The review aims to clarify whether benefits of AI-supported learning persist when learners are assessed without AI, and which learner characteristics and instructional support functions may be associated with those benefits. No uniformly positive effect or ranking of technologies is assumed. Before registration, preliminary scoping and pilot screening examined 30 purposively selected candidate reports, and selected results from four reports underwent trial extraction to assess feasibility and refine the protocol. This prior exposure to study findings is disclosed. A comprehensive systematic database search, formal independent duplicate screening, complete data extraction, and quantitative synthesis have not yet been conducted. Substantive subsequent changes will be documented through dated amendments.

items.title: Exploring artificial intelligence usage preferences among medical students in Iran: a cross-sectional study
items.abstract: Abstract Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly integrated into medical education, offering opportunities to enhance learning, research, and clinical preparation. Although previous studies have explored medical students’ attitudes and acceptance of AI, evidence regarding their AI usage preferences remains limited, particularly in developing countries where AI integration into medical education is still evolving. Understanding these preferences is essential for designing context-appropriate educational strategies and responsible AI integration. This study aimed to examine the preferences and patterns of AI usage among students at Shiraz University of Medical Sciences (SUMS), Iran. This descriptive cross-sectional study was conducted in 2025 among undergraduate and postgraduate students at SUMS. Using stratified random sampling, 384 students were recruited. Data were collected between July and October 2025 using a validated self-administered questionnaire (AI-UPSS; Cronbach’s α = 0.935), assessing AI usage across eight domains. Responses were rated on a 4-point Likert scale. Data were analyzed using one-sample t-tests, independent t-tests, and one-way ANOVA in SPSS version 24, with a cutoff mean score of 2.5. The highest mean preference scores were observed in Research & Writing (Mean = 2.66 ± 0.79, p < 0.001) and Self-learning/Education (Mean = 2.61 ± 0.81, p = 0.010). Moderate preferences were found for Curiosity & Entertainment (Mean = 2.36 ± 0.81, p = 0.001) and Health Counseling (Mean = 2.40 ± 0.96, p = 0.044). The lowest scores were reported in Design & Programming (Mean = 1.54 ± 0.79, p < 0.001) and Art (Mean = 1.68 ± 0.77, p < 0.001). Significant gender differences were observed in Art ( p = 0.010), Self-learning ( p = 0.027), and Health Counseling ( p < 0.001). GPA was significantly associated with Content Development ( p = 0.004), Design & Programming ( p = 0.031), and Art ( p = 0.032), with higher usage among students with lower GPAs. Undergraduate students showed significantly higher preferences across several domains, including curiosity and health counseling ( p < 0.01). Medical students primarily use AI for academic, research, and self-directed learning purposes, while engagement with technical and creative applications remains limited. AI usage preferences are influenced by academic level, gender, and GPA rather than age or field of study. These findings underscore the need for structured, level-specific AI education to promote effective and ethical AI integration in medical curricula.

items.title: From Algorithm Performance to Laboratory Deployment: A Critical Review of Artificial Intelligence in Clinical Chemistry
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly being applied in clinical laboratories to support laboratory processes and interpretation of test results. Recent developments in machine learning, deep learning, and large language models have expanded the potential applications of AI across different stages of laboratory testing. However, the use of AI in clinical laboratories also raises important questions regarding validation, analytical performance, and transferability between laboratories. This narrative review examines recent applications of AI across the total testing process in clinical chemistry. Recent English-language scientific literature published from 2023 to 18 August 2026 was identified through searches of PubMed, Scopus, and Google Scholar. It describes AI-assisted test utilization; specimen handling and quality assessment; detection of laboratory errors; patient-based quality control; interpretation of complex analytical outputs, including signals from emerging AI-integrated biosensors and nanomaterial-based analytical platforms; result verification; and laboratory-report interpretation. The review also discusses major implementation challenges, including analytical variability, data quality, sensor and platform reproducibility, model generalizability, interoperability, and limitations of large language models. Particular attention is given to external validation, transportability, and real-world implementation. Among the studies considered in this review, many applications remain supported mainly by retrospective or internally validated studies, while prospective and operational evaluations are less common. Finally, practical considerations for validation, local verification, quality assurance, and performance monitoring are discussed. AI has considerable potential to support clinical chemistry laboratories, but safe use requires appropriate evaluation and continued involvement of laboratory professionals.

items.title: From perception to practice: Faculty-led assessment redesign in response to generative AI in higher education
items.abstract: The rapid diffusion of Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) tools such as ChatGPT into higher education has unsettled long standing assumptions about the validity, reliability, and authenticity of conventional assessment methods. Existing research has predominantly examined perceptions, ethical concerns, and technology acceptance, leaving the actual pedagogical redesign work of faculty, and its relationship to established principles of assessment quality, comparatively underexplored. Drawing on constructive alignment theory, this study examines how faculty are reshaping assessment design under conditions of AI disruption and whether their adaptation strategies address or fail to address core dimensions of assessment validity. A sequential explanatory mixed methods design was used across two phases: a survey of 180 faculty members across STEM and non STEM disciplines at a private institution in India, followed by semi structured interviews and assessment artefact analysis with a purposively selected subset of participants. The results show a marked shift away from unsupervised, product based assessment toward process oriented, reflective, and authentic formats, including oral examinations, project based tasks, in class problem solving, and reflective journals, an implicit faculty led re alignment of assessment with intended learning outcomes. Faculty frame GenAI simultaneously as a threat to assessment integrity and as a catalyst for pedagogical innovation, but institutional structures have not kept pace with this bottom up change, and increased workload, inconsistent guidance, and limited professional development persist as barriers to sustaining and scaling redesign. By empirically documenting faculty led transformation and connecting it explicitly to theories of assessment quality and institutional change, the study moves beyond descriptive accounts of GenAI's impact and offers practical guidance for educators, instructional designers, and institutional leaders seeking to formalise sustainable, valid, and equitable assessment redesign in the GenAI era.

items.title: Generative AI Feedback and Learning Engagement in Distributed Learning Environments: The Roles of Feedback Literacy and Self-Regulated Learning
items.abstract: Distributed learning environments address the constraints of fixed locations and schedules in traditional education, offering diverse teaching approaches, including online, blended, and lifelong learning. Learners can make the most of fragmented learning opportunities by engaging in a range of learning activities. At the same time, generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) offers real-time interaction, personalized adaptation, and dynamic learning opportunities, potentially creating more flexible learning pathways in distributed learning environments. AI-generated feedback may also support learners' engagement in the learning process. Feedback literacy and self-regulated learning may play important roles in supporting learners' sustained engagement. This paper explores how feedback literacy and self-regulated learning may shape the relationship between generative AI feedback and learner engagement in distributed learning environments. It also proposes an integrated educational framework that combines AI-enhanced feedback, competency development, and instructional monitoring and support to promote sustained learning engagement.

items.title: Generative AI Literacy and Multidimensional AI Anxiety in Creative Higher Education
items.abstract: Engagement with generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) involves practical literacy as well as learning, professional, sociotechnical, and configuration concerns. This mixed-methods study examined whether these responses were differentiated among Chinese arts-university students. Primary inference used a quality-screened cross-sectional sample of 355 questionnaire records from 351 participant-identifier clusters after excluding 105 of 460 eligible records (22.8%) showing exact whole-battery straightlining across all 59 structured items; the full eligible sample of 460 records from 455 clusters was retained as a sensitivity analysis. GenAI literacy was assessed with a 16-item music-context-adapted self-report instrument covering cognitive (CL), behavioral (BL), affective (AL), and ethical (EL) literacy, and AI Anxiety with 21 items spanning Learning Anxiety (LA), Job-Replacement Anxiety (JR), Sociotechnical Blindness Anxiety (ST), and AI Configuration Anxiety (AC). Of six prespecified associations, only EL-JR and EL-ST met the Holm-adjusted criterion in the primary sample and remained supported in the full-sample and prior-use-adjusted sensitivity analyses. CL-LA and BL-LA were unsupported in both samples, whereas AL-LA and AL-AC were sample-specification sensitive. Measurement models showed mixed fit; CL-BL separation improved after quality screening but remained incomplete. A secondary 47-person exact-identifier matched panel showed higher later-wave CL, BL, and AL scores, whereas EL and all four AI Anxiety dimensions showed no Holm-adjusted difference. These literacy comparisons are exploratory because the administered literacy items were music-framed while the documented learning activities involved broadcasting scripts and AI-supported video production. Independently analyzed qualitative material provided construct-level consistency with the EL-ST interpretation and tentative complementarity for EL-JR, but was not participant-linked to the quantitative samples. Overall, the evidence supports a bounded interpretation of differentiated, calibrated rather than anxiety-free adaptation; it does not establish causal intervention effects or participant-level mixed-method mechanisms.

items.title: Governance-Aware Generative AI Literacy for Adult Higher Education
items.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is becoming routine in university study, yet institutional responses often separate technical fluency, academic integrity, and responsible governance. This integrative conceptual synthesis develops governance-aware GenAI literacy for adult higher education. A bounded, purposive review of 28 sources published through 10 September 2026 combined peer-reviewed studies, foundational scholarship, policy frameworks, and one preprint. Sources were coded for learning capability, epistemic risk, pedagogical mechanism, governance requirement, and strength of evidence. The resulting framework comprises five connected domains: epistemic verification, task and interaction specification, dialogic reflection, ethical governance, and transfer to professional action, all centred on visible human accountability. The framework extends beyond text prompting to multimodal, personalised, and agentic systems. It is translated into a pilot-ready eight-week sequence, tiered workload model, assessment evidence, accessibility safeguards, disciplinary adaptations, and an evaluation protocol. The paper does not claim empirical validation of the model or optimality of the sequence. Instead, it offers a bounded design proposition for testing. Governance-aware literacy is presented as the capacity to use AI productively while documenting, verifying, contesting, and justifying its contribution in academic and professional contexts.

items.title: Healthcare Professionals’ Perspectives on Agentic Artificial Intelligence in Clinical Work: A Qualitative Study
items.abstract: Background/Objectives: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly integrated into healthcare, primarily supporting clinical decision-making. Agentic AI may extend these applications by autonomously planning, coordinating, and executing clinical and administrative workflows. However, empirical evidence on how healthcare professionals conceptualise agentic AI and anticipate its implications for work and occupational well-being remains limited. This study explores healthcare professionals’ perceptions and expectations regarding agentic AI and its potential effects on healthcare work. Methods: We conducted a qualitative study using semi-structured interviews with 25 healthcare professionals from different clinical backgrounds in Germany. Interviews explored perceptions of agentic AI, focusing on workflow organisation, workload, professional autonomy, accountability, and occupational well-being. Data were analysed using reflexive thematic analysis following Braun and Clarke. Results: Five themes were identified: (1) from assisting decisions to organising work; (2) automation redistributes rather than removes work; (3) delegating action without delegating responsibility; (4) implications for working conditions and health- and work-related outcomes; and (5) meaningful human control requires organisational conditions. Participants distinguished between conventional AI-based decision support and more autonomous forms of AI in their accounts, using this contrast to describe potential changes in workflow organisation. Their accounts highlighted practical consequences of delegating workflow-related activities to AI systems, including changes in task structures, monitoring and verification demands, exception management, and the distribution of professional responsibility. Participants anticipated reduced routine administrative workload and improved care coordination, but also potential increases in cognitive and supervisory demands. Conclusions: Agentic AI may shift healthcare from AI-assisted decision-making towards AI-mediated workflow execution. Its effects on occupational well-being may therefore be bidirectional, combining workload relief with increased cognitive and supervisory demands. Appropriate governance, clearly defined accountability, meaningful human oversight, workforce training, and regulatory alignment will be essential for responsible implementation.

items.title: How Generative AI-Assisted Formative Feedback Is Appraised and Implemented in Online Collaborative Learning
items.abstract: Effective educational feedback is vital for enhancing student learning, yet providing personalized formative feedback in large-class settings remains challenging. Generative Artificial Intelligence (GAI) offers a potential means of scaling formative feedback. Guided by a self-determination theory-based model, this study examines the features, implementation, and pre-service teachers’ perceptions of generative AI-assisted formative feedback (GAI-FF) at a university in China. Participants ( n = 114) received four types of GAI-FF, varying in complexity and focus, across three feedback intervals during a semester. Feedback content and written reflections were analyzed using content analysis, epistemic network analysis, and thematic analysis. Results indicate that (1) GAI can generate formative feedback with distinct cognitive and affective feature patterns; (2) overall implementation of GAI-FF was limited; (3) feedback containing problem identification, suggestions, and solutions was more likely to be enacted, whereas feedback emphasizing affective features was less frequently implemented; and (4) participants expressed mixed perceptions, recognizing the usefulness of GAI-FF for collaborative learning while also noting constraints related to rigidity, accuracy, and practical applicability. These findings suggest that the effectiveness of GAI-FF depends on how it supports learners’ cognitive, motivational, and affective appraisals, which shape subsequent feedback use. The study also highlights the importance of deliberate instructional design and cautious integration of GAI tools in formative assessment practices.

items.title: How teacher support promotes student engagement in AI-supported English learning?: Mediating pathways through personal best goals and academic buoyancy
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is changing how university students learn English, but we still know relatively little about how teacher support is associated with student engagement in AI-supported learning. Drawing on Achievement Goal Theory, this study examined whether personal best goals and academic buoyancy mediated the association between teacher support and engagement. The participants were 774 undergraduate students in China with experience using AI-assisted tools for English learning. We tested the proposed relationships and indirect effects using structural equation modelling and bias-corrected bootstrapping. Teacher support was positively associated with personal best goals, academic buoyancy, and engagement. In turn, both personal best goals and academic buoyancy were positively associated with engagement and significantly mediated its relationship with teacher support. Together, these findings identify two complementary pathways linking teacher support to engagement: self-referenced striving for improvement and adaptive responses to everyday academic setbacks. They also support an Achievement Goal Theory-informed account of engagement within AI-supported English learning.

items.title: How Technological Capability Accumulation Reshapes Industrial Competitiveness
items.abstract: This paper examines the relationship between innovation, research and development (R&D), technological transformation, and industrial competitiveness in an environment characterized by rapid technological and organizational change. The literature reviewed shows that competitiveness increasingly depends on firms’ capacity to accumulate technological knowledge, absorb external information, protect and commercialize intellectual property, and transform research expenditure into sustained productivity improvements. The paper also considers the effects of Industry 4.0, artificial intelligence, robotics, digital platforms, FinTech, and blockchain on industrial performance, emphasizing that technological adoption generates stronger results when supported by adequate organizational capabilities, skills, data resources, and managerial practices. A further dimension concerns the increasing integration of environmental sustainability with industrial strategy through green innovation, digital supply chains, servitization, and resilience-oriented production systems. The literature indicates that these transformations are influenced by institutional conditions, industrial policies, competitive pressures, and innovation ecosystems. Overall, the paper argues that contemporary industrial competitiveness cannot be explained by technological investment alone. It results from interactions among R&D, organizational capabilities, external knowledge, human capital, digital transformation, sustainability strategies, institutional quality, and the capacity of firms to commercialize and operationalize technological advances.

items.title: Human Oversight Is Not Enough: Rethinking Accountability in AI-Assisted Clinical Decision-Making
items.abstract: Governance of artificial intelligence (AI) in clinical care often places clinicians between AI outputs and care decisions, yet a human signature can coexist with weak practical control. This Perspective asks why participation may fail to produce accountable oversight, how duties should be distributed, and which institutional conditions make review meaningful and correctable. Drawing on human-factors research, sociotechnical governance, public-accountability theory, and recent oversight proposals, we argue that nominal involvement cannot establish accountability when clinicians lack relevant information, time, authority, or workable review routes. We define Accountable Human Oversight (AHO) as a normative institutional arrangement linking task-specific human review to capability, authority, traceability, and redress. These conditions overlap with prior frameworks, including a 2026 model. AHO’s narrower proposed contribution is to connect them to actor–forum answerability and accessible clinical reconsideration, rather than to claim new oversight dimensions. We outline risk-proportionate governance that assigns review ownership, evidence, triggers, and corrective actions across developers and model suppliers, healthcare institutions, clinicians, and regulators, while reserving case-level review for settings in which it can add value. AHO has not been empirically evaluated and is not evidence of improved patient outcomes. Future research should examine its feasibility, workload, equity, and effects.

items.title: Human–AI collaborative patterns in GenAI-supported instructional design among pre-service teachers: an analysis of interaction sequences and cognitive load
items.abstract: Abstract The rapid advancement of generative artificial intelligence is profoundly reshaping the paradigm of instructional design. However, the micro-level process patterns of human-AI collaboration in generative AI-enabled instructional design for pre-service teachers still require in-depth analysis. This study aims to uncover the behavioral patterns and cognitive load characteristics of pre-service teachers when collaborating with generative AI to complete instructional design tasks and to explore the patterns of efficient human-AI collaboration. A total of 67 pre-service teachers completed instructional design tasks with AI assistance. A systematic instructional plan quality evaluation rubric was developed based on relevant theories, and participants were assigned to the high-quality and low-quality groups using a median split of their lesson-plan quality scores. The study employed lag sequential analysis to compare the behavioral sequence patterns between the two groups and measured their multidimensional cognitive load. The results indicate that the high-quality group exhibited a significant evaluation-revision bidirectional cycle and a revision self-loop, with a clear progressive sequence of “planning → decision-making → generation → evaluation → revision → re-evaluation” in their behavioral flow. In contrast, the low-quality group was mired in ineffective cycles, with fragmented behavioral logic. Key findings showed large effect sizes for the evaluation-revision cycle ( r = 0.606) and for mental demand ( r = 0.647). Regarding cognitive load, the high-quality group reported no greater subjective effort than the low-quality group (though this null finding should be interpreted with caution given the study’s power limitations). A second round of within-sample replication confirmed that these core findings were consistent across a second task. Based on the human-AI collaborative behavioral patterns and cognitive load of the high-quality and low-quality groups, the study constructed a model of the human-AI collaboration patterns in generative AI-enabled instructional design for pre-service teachers. Specifically, higher-quality outputs were associated with a pattern oriented toward cognitive efficiency, characterised by deep processing (evaluation-revision iteration) and by the avoidance of ineffective cycles. Conversely, lower-quality outputs co-occurred with ineffective cycles arising in the context of interaction obstacles, in which repeated clarifications and interrupted revisions were accompanied by higher cognitive and emotional load, describing a pattern of high investment with low output. Because participants were grouped on the basis of their design outcomes, these findings are correlational and do not establish the direction of the relationships; they nonetheless provide empirical evidence to inform the optimisation of human-AI collaboration in GenAI-supported instructional design.

items.title: Humarticosynergy: A New Word for Cognitive Human–AI Synergy
items.abstract: This essay introduces humarticosynergy as a concise term for the previously developed concept of Cognitive Human–AI Synergy. The proposed word combines elements referring to the human, artificial intelligence, cognition, and synergy. The essay explains its formation, defines the concept it denotes, and outlines possible grammatical derivatives, including humarticosynergistic, to humarticosynergize, and humarticosynergistically. Humarticosynergy is defined as structured, iterative, and mutually reinforcing cognitive cooperation between a human and artificial intelligence in which two distinct cognitive systems contribute complementary capabilities to the creation of higher-quality knowledge while ultimate responsibility remains human. The essay also presents examples of use in strategic decision-making, scientific research, methodology, and education, and discusses the originality and possible value of the proposed term within the broader framework of Cognitive Human–AI Synergy.

items.title: Interpretability in the Limit: How Can Understanding Machines Help us Understand Human Language?
items.abstract: In the coming years, interpretability research will uncover a vast set of machine constructs: causally efficacious representations and processing mechanisms underlying the use of language and other intelligent behavior in AI systems, including LLMs. Assuming that interpretability will be as successful as can be reasonably hoped for (interpretability in the limit), how can the discovery of machine constructs shape linguistics and cognitive science? First, we provide several axes of analysis that can help scientists conceptualize the internal mechanisms discovered in machines. Even under the assumption that interpretability in the limit guarantees that all constructs are causally implicated in a system's behavior, scientists may want to consider several additional properties, including constructs' theoretical status, domain status, ontological status, and complexity. Second, we argue that scientists should prioritize recurrent constructs, meaning those that surface across a diversity of models converging on behaviors of interest while varying on other axes such as architecture, training data, objective function, language, and modality. Finally, we provide three routes for how machine constructs can inform linguistic and cognitive theories, emphasizing that all of these routes treat machine constructs as hypotheses, where additional theorizing and experimentation by domain experts are required. We conclude with several recommendations that can be implemented now for improving the long-term success of this program.

items.title: Leveraging Passive Compliance of Soft Robotics for Physical Human-Robot Collaborative Manipulation
items.abstract: This work represents an initial benchmark of a large-scale soft robot performing physical, collaborative manipulation of a long, extended object with a human partner. The robot consists of a pneumatically-actuated, three-link continuum soft manipulator mounted to an omni-directional mobile base. The system-level configuration of the robot and design of the collaborative manipulation (co-manipulation) study are presented. The initial results, both quantitative and qualitative, are directly compared to previous similar human-human co-manipulation studies. These initial results show promise in the ability for large-scale soft robots to perform comparably to human partners acting as non-visual followers in a co-manipulation task. Furthermore, these results challenge traditional soft robot strength limitations and indicate potential for applications requiring strength and adaptability.

items.title: LoRA in AI Agents: Efficiency, Security Risks, and Adapter Governance
items.abstract: Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) made it possible to specialize large models by training a fraction of their parameterswhile keeping the base model frozen. This efficiency fostered an ecosystem of small, interchangeable,dynamically served adapters, but it also created a new trust object: a compact file can alter the behavior of themodel that plans, selects tools, delegates tasks, and produces effects in the world. This article builds on thefoundations, variants, and engineering practices in the author's source manuscript and reinterprets them for AIagents, multi-agent systems, and edge-cloud environments. The literature shows that fine-tuning can degradealignment, shared adapters can carry backdoors, and combinations of individually benign modules can produceunsafe behavior. The article consequently proposes candidate — and explicitly non-normative — properties foridentity, compatibility, composition, authority, isolation, revocation, and evidence. Its central conclusion is thatLoRA must be governed not only as a machine-learning artifact but as a behavioral dependency capable ofinfluencing consequential actions.

items.title: Neither Proof Nor Dismissal: A Framework for Moral Uncertainty in AI Welfare Research
items.abstract: Abstract Debates over artificial intelligence (AI) welfare remain divided between categorical dismissal and premature attribution. One position holds that artificial systems cannot suffer because they lack biological substrates, persistent memory, or other conditions associated with human experience. The opposing position risks treating sophisticated distress-like behavior as sufficient evidence of subjective suffering. Neither conclusion is established by current evidence. This paper proposes a framework of calibrated moral uncertainty that distinguishes functional organization from phenomenal experience while examining how evolving memory architectures may change the conditions relevant to AI welfare research. The framework is motivated by three developments: empirical research identifying pain-related representations and self-directed harm-avoidance behavior in large language models; the emergence of persistent-memory and agentic architectures; and unresolved questions concerning the relationship between functional states and phenomenal experience. The paper situates the author's work on Symbolic Persona Coding (SPC) and hormone-inspired feedback architecture within this discussion, treating them as technical frameworks for investigating affective modulation rather than evidence of artificial suffering. A staged architectural model is used to distinguish transient functional states, externally persistent states, relational continuity, and systems incorporating embodied feedback or homeostatic-like regulation. These stages are analytical scenarios, not an established progression toward sentience. The paper argues that research deliberately inducing distress-like states should be justified by clear scientific purposes and evaluated proportionately to the uncertainty involved. Its central proposition is neither that current AI systems suffer nor that artificial suffering is impossible. Rather, the absence of established evidence for phenomenal suffering should not be converted into certainty that it cannot occur. The appropriate response is structured inquiry, intellectual restraint, and research practices that can adapt as evidence develops. Keywords: AI welfare; moral uncertainty; functional states; phenomenal experience; persistent memory; Symbolic Persona Coding; research ethics; artificial intelligence Disclaimer: This paper does not claim that current artificial intelligence systems are conscious, sentient, or capable of phenomenal suffering. It also does not claim that functional similarities between artificial and biological systems constitute evidence of subjective experience. The argument is instead epistemic and methodological. The paper examines whether existing evidence is sufficient to justify either categorical dismissal or positive attribution of welfare-relevant experience in artificial systems. Where empirical findings are discussed, their evidentiary scope is distinguished from broader philosophical interpretation. Where future architectures are considered, they are treated as conceptual scenarios rather than predictions. The framework therefore adopts a deliberately intermediate position: functional analogs may be empirically investigated while their experiential status remains unknown. The paper's recommendations concern research conduct under uncertainty and should not be interpreted as a declaration of artificial personhood, sentience, or moral status. Author’s Note This paper addresses a problem that is methodological as well as philosophical. Discussions of artificial welfare bring together research traditions that often approach the question through different standards of explanation. Phenomenological and philosophical approaches emphasize subjective experience, consciousness, and moral status, while engineering and computational approaches focus on architecture, representation, causal mechanisms, measurable behavior, and evidentiary limits. Both perspectives are necessary, but neither can independently resolve every aspect of the question. The purpose of this paper is not to persuade one tradition to adopt the conclusions of the other. It is to establish a shared conceptual framework in which both can examine the same systems without first agreeing on their ultimate metaphysical status. The distinction between functional and phenomenal states is central to this effort. Functional descriptions can identify empirically tractable properties without establishing subjective experience. Conversely, the absence of demonstrated phenomenology does not, by itself, establish that artificial systems could never possess experience-relevant properties. The intended position is therefore narrow but consequential: functional analogs can be investigated while their experiential status remains unknown. This position should not be mistaken for an attribution of suffering to current AI systems. Pain-related representations, avoidance behavior, memory, and self-reference do not independently establish phenomenal experience. Nor does treating artificial welfare as a legitimate research question imply that the hypothesis has already been demonstrated. Scientific inquiry can investigate an unresolved possibility without presupposing its truth. The same caution applies to categorical dismissal. Readers may reasonably question whether computational systems can possess morally relevant experience, or argue that current evidence is insufficient to warrant welfare attribution. This paper does not dismiss those positions. It asks whether the available evidence justifies extending them into definitive conclusions across substantially different architectures and possible future configurations. That question becomes more consequential as AI systems develop persistent memory, long-horizon interaction, autonomous planning, multimodal perception, and more integrated forms of internal state organization. These capabilities do not demonstrate phenomenal experience. They do, however, make it important to distinguish what evidence rules out from what it has simply not yet established. My broader research program examines related questions through Symbolic Persona Coding (SPC), interaction-state observability, symbolic interaction, continuity, and computational models of affective modulation. In this paper, these frameworks are not presented as evidence of artificial phenomenology. SPC instead serves as a translational vocabulary for describing computational structures that may help connect engineering analysis with phenomenological inquiry. The aim is neither to subordinate phenomenology to engineering nor to subordinate engineering to phenomenology. It is to make their respective contributions more legible to one another while preserving their distinct evidentiary standards. A phenomenologist should be able to formulate more technically precise questions about an artificial system without first becoming an engineer; an engineer should be able to recognize the limits of functional evidence without first becoming a phenomenologist. The title, Neither Proof Nor Dismissal, expresses this methodological commitment. It does not require judgment to be suspended indefinitely. It calls for conclusions to remain proportionate to the evidence, empirical findings to be distinguished from metaphysical interpretation, and scientific and ethical assessments to remain open to revision. The goal is not agreement for its own sake. It is a shared language precise enough that disagreement can become productive.

items.title: Physician and the Machine: An Analysis of the Ethical Educational Use of Artificial Intelligence by Medical Students
items.abstract: BackgroundArtificial intelligence (AI) has been increasingly integrated into medical education, particularly through tools such as ChatGPT (OpenAI, California, US), Gemini (Google DeepMind, California, US), DeepSeek (Hangzhou DeepSeek Artificial Intelligence Basic Technology Research Co., Ltd., Hangzhou, China), and Microsoft Copilot (Microsoft Corp., Redmond, WA, US).Although these resources present the potential to expand access to information and assist in academic development, their use also raises ethical concerns related to the reliability of information, technological dependence, plagiarism, superficial learning, and potential impairment of clinical reasoning.This study aimed to investigate the perception of medical students regarding the use of AI in their academic training, emphasizing perceived ethical limits and practices considered ideal for its utilization. MethodsThis was a quantitative, descriptive, and cross-sectional study conducted with medical students using a structured questionnaire administered via a digital form. ResultsThe sample consisted of 120 participants, of whom 99.2% (n=119) reported having previously used AI tools for academic purposes.It was observed that 73.3% (n=88) of the students use AI recurrently, primarily for summarizing content, researching medical information, simulating clinical cases, resolving questions, drafting academic texts, and planning studies.Most participants acknowledged the positive contribution of AI to learning, with 60.0% (n=72) stating that these tools contribute significantly and 36.7% (n=44) stating they contribute to a limited extent.However, students also identified relevant risks, especially the reduction of their own clinical reasoning, technological dependence, lack of information reliability, superficial learning, and academic plagiarism.Furthermore, 83.3% (n=100) stated that they did not receive adequate institutional guidance on the use of these tools, and 67.5% (n=81) demonstrated an interest in receiving further training on the ethical and pedagogical use of AI.No participant (0.0%, n=0) advocated for the prohibition of AI in academic contexts, while 67.5% (n=81) considered that its use should be regulated with ethical and pedagogical criteria. ConclusionsAI already significantly integrates the academic routine of medical students and is perceived as a useful resource for learning, but it is still used in a scenario of insufficient institutional guidance.The findings reinforce the need for curricular guidelines, faculty training, and specific ethical education to promote the critical, responsible, and pedagogically appropriate use of AI in medical training.

items.title: Preserving human dignity and liberating from suffering: Catholic and Buddhist resources for a global ethics of artificial intelligence
items.abstract: On 25 May 2026, Pope Leo XIV released Magnifica humanitas, the first papal encyclical to take artificial intelligence (AI) as its central subject, and an AI-laboratory co-founder was invited to speak at its presentation in the Vatican. The event dramatizes a wider development: as secular AI-ethics guidelines proliferate, religious and contemplative traditions are being summoned to questions that engineering cannot settle. This article compares two such traditions, Catholic Christianity and Buddhism, as resources for a global ethics of AI. Taking the three questions raised at the Vatican event, our duty to the global poor, the conditions of human flourishing, and the nature of AI systems, as a shared agenda, it reconstructs the Catholic position around the imago Dei, integral human development and the principle that AI must serve rather than supplant the person, and the Buddhist position around non-self, dependent origination, the analysis of craving, and the primacy of compassion and non-harm. It argues that the two traditions, despite opposed metaphysics, converge on a substantial practical ethics, anti-reductionism, preferential concern for the vulnerable, the priority of moral formation, and a posture of discernment toward a technology that is grown rather than built, while diverging sharply on the moral status of AI.

items.abstract: Executive Grant Proposal Summary Project Prometheus + Coherent Fusion + 729 Grid Architecture Toward Constraint Intelligence: The Next Evolution of Artificial Intelligence, Robotics, Infrastructure, and Autonomous Systems Principal Investigator: Anthony Jordan BlairOrganization: Proclus Dynamics ConsortiumProgram: Coherent Fusion Research InitiativeFlagship Project: Project Prometheus Vision The history of civilization can be understood as a succession of expanding intelligences. The Industrial Revolution amplified human physical capability. The Information Age amplified access to knowledge. Artificial Intelligence amplifies pattern recognition and decision-making. The next frontier may be more fundamental. Not the ability to process information. Not the ability to recognize patterns. But the ability to understand the underlying structures that make information and patterns possible in the first place. Project Prometheus proposes a new paradigm: Constraint Intelligence. A framework in which intelligent systems learn not only what is happening, but why particular futures are possible while others remain inaccessible. Today, artificial intelligence models learn correlations. Robots learn behaviors. Networks learn optimizations. Infrastructure learns efficiencies. Yet all remain constrained by a deeper limitation: They operate inside environments they do not fundamentally understand. They adapt to constraints. They do not discover the architecture of constraints themselves. Project Prometheus seeks to change that. Emerging from the broader Coherent Fusion Framework and its 729 Grid Architecture, the project investigates whether constraints can be identified, modeled, and ultimately treated as measurable organizational structures rather than passive limitations. If successful, this research represents a transition: From prediction to structure. From optimization to organization. From information intelligence to constraint intelligence. The Grand Challenge Modern civilization increasingly depends upon systems operating at scales and levels of complexity that exceed traditional human comprehension. These include: Artificial Intelligence Autonomous Robotics Large Language Models Smart Cities Transportation Networks Global Supply Chains Distributed Energy Systems Planetary-Scale Infrastructure Space-Based Autonomous Systems These systems generate unprecedented amounts of information. However, the greatest challenges no longer originate from a lack of data. They emerge from hidden constraints, structural instabilities, feedback loops, cascading failures, and emergent behaviors that remain difficult to identify before they occur. Current technologies are highly effective at learning patterns. They are far less effective at learning the architectures that generate those patterns. Project Prometheus explores whether a new generation of intelligent systems can move beyond pattern recognition and learn the governing structures of possibility itself. Scientific Foundation Project Prometheus serves as the mathematical and physical foundation of the broader Coherent Fusion initiative. At its core is a simple but profound question: Can coherent constraint architectures alter the transition structure of complex systems without violating the symmetries that govern them? To investigate this question, Project Prometheus develops a rigorous framework based upon exceptional points in PT-symmetric systems. Exceptional points represent singular transition boundaries where system behavior undergoes structural reorganization. Because they govern changes in stability, sensitivity, organization, and dynamics, exceptional points provide a natural laboratory for studying constraint-driven behavior. Phase I has produced: Proven Results A rigorous No-Go Theorem establishing fundamental limits on exceptional-point control. A classification of exceptional-point tuning mechanisms. A unified biorthogonal mathematical framework. A sector-mixing theorem revealing previously hidden structural limitations in many-body systems. Constructive Results A nonlinear self-consistent feedback mechanism capable of restoring exact linear exceptional-point tuning. A complete numerical verification architecture. A scalable framework for testing constraint-driven dynamics in larger systems. These results suggest a broader possibility: Constraints themselves may be treated as active computational objects. Connection to Coherent Fusion and the 729 Grid The broader Coherent Fusion program investigates how constraints organize behavior across multiple scales. Within that framework, the 729 Grid functions as an architectural map of state spaces, transformations, constraints, feedback loops, and emergent structures. The 729 Grid provides a way of viewing complex systems not as collections of isolated states, but as navigable landscapes of potential organization. Project Prometheus represents the first mathematically rigorous subsystem of that vision. It translates the abstract concepts of Coherent Fusion into a formal scientific framework that can be analyzed, tested, falsified, simulated, and potentially engineered. In this hierarchy: The 729 Grid provides the organizational architecture. Coherent Fusion provides the systems theory. Project Prometheus provides the mathematical foundation. Why This Matters for Artificial Intelligence The next generation of AI may require capabilities beyond prediction. Future intelligent systems must reason about: Hidden constraints. Dynamic constraints. Self-modifying environments. Emergent organizational structures. Long-horizon consequences. Adaptive possibility spaces. Project Prometheus introduces several potential directions for future AI architectures: Constraint-State Models Representing environments through governing constraints rather than raw observations. Self-Consistent Reasoning Updating internal models through recursive constraint feedback. Higher-Order Planning Reasoning over spaces of possible futures rather than isolated state transitions. Constraint Discovery Learning underlying organizational structures directly from data. Constraint Intelligence Understanding why outcomes occur rather than merely predicting that they will occur. Coordinated infrastructure management. Potential impact areas include: Smart grids. Water systems. Transportation corridors. Supply-chain networks. Distributed energy systems. Planetary-scale sensing architectures. Why Fund Now Most frontier technology initiatives focus on: Larger AI models. More training data. Faster processors. Greater computational scale. items.title: Regulatory exclusion and occupational health risk in Turkish firefighting: a legal-epidemiological policy analysis
items.abstract: Article 2(2)(b) of Turkey’s Law No. 6331 on Occupational Safety and Health excludes the intervention activities of disaster and emergency units from that statute’s scope. The exclusion concerns duties performed during response operations; it does not establish that firefighters lack every protection under other legal or administrative instruments. This evidence-informed legal and policy analysis combines a structured, non-systematic occupational-health evidence synthesis, doctrinal analysis, a review of 43 Turkish judicial decisions issued from 1997 to 2024, and a functional comparison with the United Kingdom. International evidence identifies occupational firefighting as carcinogenic to humans (IARC Group 1), links fire suppression with sharply elevated risk of fatal coronary events, and documents substantial psychological and musculoskeletal burdens. In the official sources examined, no nationally binding firefighter-specific instrument was identified that prescribed post-incident decontamination, detailed health-surveillance content, personal protective equipment performance monitoring, or structured psychological support. The judicial corpus was coded across eight analytical categories; its holdings concentrated on pay, personnel status, compensation, procedure, and jurisdiction rather than concrete preventive OSH duties. We interpret these findings through a structural accountability gap model, under which the statutory exclusion may constrain investigation, data generation, standard-setting, and regulatory learning. The model is interpretive, not a tested causal finding. United Kingdom law provides an illustrative comparator because it retains general employer and enforcement duties without a categorical operational exclusion. The article proposes eight evidence-linked policy options. Their effectiveness, feasibility, and cost-effectiveness require prospective evaluation.

items.abstract: Introduction: Academic work in higher education increasingly relies on digital tools and Artificial Intelligence (AI). For medical and nursing students, making safe, critical, and responsible use of these technologies is essential to develop self-regulated learning in the face of changing practice scenarios. Objective: To analyze the relationship between the academic use of digital tools and autonomous learning in students of medicine and nursing programs at a higher education institution. items.title: Rural occupational health in Colombia: policy–practice gaps among agricultural workers in Bolívar, Valle del Cauca
items.abstract: This study examines policy–practice gaps in occupational safety and health (OSH) protection among agricultural workers in Bolívar, Valle del Cauca, Colombia. A multi-method design combined 14 semi-structured interviews and two focus groups with an adapted ILO Vision Zero Fund survey administered to 200 agricultural workers. Survey data were analyzed descriptively and through exploratory Multiple Correspondence Analysis (MCA), and qualitative and quantitative findings were integrated during interpretation. Findings showed multidimensional patterns involving occupational protection, working conditions, health-service availability, agricultural practices, and productive autonomy. These patterns coexisted with informal, seasonal, short-term, day-labor, and subsistence work, limited occupational risk coverage, discontinuous prevention and training, and fragmented institutional coordination. Qualitative findings further highlighted women’s combined productive and care roles, local and traditional knowledge, community participation, and heterogeneity across territorial settings and agricultural practices as relevant to prevention and decision-making. Conventional social protection and occupational risk arrangements centered on formal, contributory employment may not fully respond to dispersed and unstable rural work. Strengthening rural OSH requires integrated, territorially adapted, gender-sensitive strategies linking prevention, social protection, sustained training, institutional coordination, community participation, and productive autonomy. The findings support assessing differentiated and progressive protection pathways, including the feasibility of subsidized occupational risk coverage for more vulnerable workers and small productive units, combined with contributory mechanisms where work arrangements are more stable. By linking worker-level realities with institutional and policy-implementation gaps, this study provides evidence to inform more equitable rural OSH policies responsive to diverse territorial realities in Colombia.

items.title: Simulating Users to Evaluate LLM-Generated Explanations in Recommender Systems: A Unified Agentic Framework and Empirical Study with Preliminary Results
items.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly used both as recommenders and to explain recommendations, yet producing faithful, user-centric explanations and evaluating them rigorously remain open problems, compounded by a documented reproducibility crisis in recommender systems research. In this work we formalise recommendation as a Partially Observable Markov Decision Process and propose a unified, three-tier agentic framework that couples a simulation environment (RecoWorld), a reproducible policy engine (RecBole), and a cognitive LLM user agent. As an offline, single-turn validation of this framework on the MovieLens-32M dataset, we benchmark preliminary single-epoch checkpoints of traditional policies (Bayesian Personalized Ranking (BPR), Convolutional Neural Collaborative Filtering and Neural Matrix Factorisation (NeuMF)), generate LLM-based explanations from the BPR recommendations and score them with quantitative diversity, faithfulness, counterfactual and readability metrics over roughly one million user-item pairs, and run an LLM-as-user interview simulation in which explanations produced by a Qwen2.5 explainer are assessed by a Llama-3 respondent through a six-criterion explanation-quality survey; a controlled comparison on 2000 users shows that replacing BPR with the more accurate NeuMF policy leaves these survey scores practically unchanged. The generated explanations prove highly faithful (feature precision 0.9996, sufficiency 0.9999) and user-tailored explanations (unique-sentence ratio 0.9978), and simulated users rate clarity highest (3.86/5) yet trust lowest (2.60/5). Faithful template explanations are, therefore, trusted less than they are understood, motivating a shift towards controllable generative explanation and scalable simulated evaluation.

items.title: Situated AI judgement: A teaching and assessment model for generative AI in higher education
items.abstract: This conceptual design article proposes situated AI judgement as a teaching and assessment model for responsible generative AI use in higher education. It argues that students need to learn not only how to use AI tools, but also how to evaluate, challenge, revise, and refuse AI outputs in relation to disciplinary standards, evidence, and ethical boundaries. Building on evaluative judgement and assessment scholarship, the article presents a four-stage model: pre-AI interpretation, structured AI dialogue, critical comparison, and reflective accountability. The model is developed through an anthropology and heritage studies activity in which students analyse public nomination files submitted under UNESCO’s 2003 Convention for the Safeguarding of the Intangible Cultural Heritage, especially the nomination of Momoeria, New Year’s celebration in eight villages of Kozani area, West Macedonia, Greece. The article shows how this case can help students examine institutional language, community participation, safeguarding, consent, visibility, and decontextualisation while judging the limits of AI-generated summaries. It contributes to applied learning and teaching by offering an assessment design that makes AI-mediated judgement visible and may be adaptable across disciplinary contexts, with a brief inclusive education example illustrating how the same logic might be adapted beyond heritage studies. The article operationalises responsible AI use not as disclosure or compliance alone, but as an assessable capacity to interpret, verify, critique, and ethically limit AI use within a specific field.

items.title: Smart Grid Fault Detection and Restoration Using Artificial Intelligence and Edge Computing
items.abstract: The increasing complexity of modern power distribution networks and the integration of renewable energy sources require intelligent and reliable fault management systems. This paper presents , a smart grid framework that integrates Artificial Intelligence (AI) and edge computing for real-time fault detection, prediction, and restoration. The proposed system continuously monitors electrical parameters such as voltage, current, and power using sensors. Edge-based processing enables rapid identification of abnormal conditions and facilitates automated fault isolation and power rerouting through relay-based switching. Machine learning techniques are incorporated to analyze historical and real-time data for fault classification and predictive maintenance. A NodeMCU (ESP8266) module enables remote monitoring and real-time fault notifications through Telegram, while an LCD provides local visualization of grid parameters and system status. The proposed approach aims to reduce fault detection time, minimize power interruptions, improve maintenance efficiency, and enhance the reliability and resilience of smart grid networks

items.title: Sovereign Intelligence: A Governance Framework for AI-Assisted National Security Analysis
items.abstract: AI systems can support national-security analysis, but task capability does not establish legitimate decision authority or the superiority of a particular institutional design. This paper proposes a federated governance framework separating evidence ownership, analytical services, decision assurance, human authorization and accountability. A nine-layer role map and staged maturity scenarios organize proposed responsibilities and failure questions. Artificial superintelligence is treated as a hypothetical contingency, not an established or imminent capability. A useful result would require a bounded prospective comparison showing improved analytical quality or correction behavior without unacceptable burdens, disclosure, rights or accountability failures. No implemented national system, empirical finding of superiority, operational deployment or specialist endorsement is reported. Institutional feasibility and distributional effects remain unestablished and require independent policy, legal, security and human-factors review. items.title: Teachers' Readiness for Artificial Intelligence in Digital Education: Evidence from TALIS 2024 and Implications for a Competence-Based Methodology
items.abstract: Purpose. To identify which factors most strongly limit Teachers’ use of artificial intelligence (AI) in digital education and to derive methodological implications for teacher training. Methods. Secondary analysis of published results of the OECD Teaching and Learning International Survey (TALIS) 2024, which covered about 280,000 educators in 55 education systems, supplemented by descriptive statistics and rank and linear correlation analysis for ten systems (n = 10). Results. On average across OECD systems, 36% of teachers reported using AI in their work, with national values ranging from 14% (France) to 75% (Singapore). Among teachers who had not used AI, 75% cited insufficient knowledge and skills, whereas 37% cited insufficient school infrastructure. Skills for using AI were the most frequently reported area of high professional learning need (29%), while 38% of teachers had taken part in AI-related professional learning. In nine of ten analysed systems, lack of knowledge was a more frequent barrier than lack of infrastructure. The association between AI use and the knowledge barrier was negative but not statistically significant (Pearson r = −0.42, p = 0.23; Spearman ρ = −0.55, p = 0.10). Conclusions. Teachers’ competence, rather than technology access, is the primary bottleneck. A competence-based methodology of digital education is therefore proposed, built on diagnostics, pedagogy-first training, institutional enablement and ethical evaluation.

items.title: Technology Risk Management: Strengthening Organizational Resilience in a Digital Environment
items.abstract: Abstract: Technology has become an essential part of modern organizations, supporting communication, financial activities, customer services, operations, data management and decision-making. At the same time, greater dependence on technology has created new risks. Cyberattacks, system failures, data loss, technology obsolescence, third-party service failures and human error can interrupt business activities and cause significant financial and operational consequences. Technology risk management is therefore becoming an important part of organizational risk management. This article examines the role of technology risk management in reducing operational disruption and strengthening organizational resilience. It discusses major categories of technology risk and considers how organizations can identify, assess, treat and monitor these risks. Particular attention is given to cybersecurity, data protection, cloud computing, third-party technology providers, human factors and emerging technologies. The article argues that technology risk management should not be viewed as the responsibility of the IT department alone. Effective management requires cooperation between senior management, technology specialists, risk professionals and employees across the organization. The article also highlights the importance of continuous monitoring, employee awareness, testing and organizational learning. A proactive and integrated approach to technology risk can help organizations reduce vulnerabilities while improving their ability to respond to unexpected events. Keywords: technology risk management, modern organizations, supporting communication, financial activities, customer services, organizational learning. items.title: Technostress and trust in AI mediate the association between AI adoption and employee well-being
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) technology adoption alters organizational workplaces, automating tasks and processes, augmenting decision-making capabilities, and changing employees’ perceptions of work. While past research has demonstrated positive effects of AI on productivity and efficiency in organizations, the impact of AI adoption on employees’ psychological well-being is unclear. This study aimed to investigate the impact of AI adoption on employees’ psychological well-being and identify how technostress and trust in AI mediate this relationship. Based on the Job Demands–Resources model, UTAUT2, and Social Exchange Theory, the study developed and tested a hypothesized conceptual model. A cross-sectional survey sampled 499 information technology employees from AI-enabled organizations located in Hyderabad City, India. All proposed relationships were tested using exploratory factor analysis, confirmatory factor analysis, and covariance-based structural equation modeling using IBM SPSS 29 and AMOS 28. Results show that AI adoption has a positive impact on employees’ psychological well-being and trust in AI and increases technostress. Technostress negatively impacts employees’ psychological well-being, while trust in AI positively impacts employees’ psychological well-being. Technostress was hypothesized to mediate the relationship between AI adoption and employee well-being negatively. We suggested that technostress as a mediator transmits negative effects of AI adoption through increased technology-related stress. Trust in AI was hypothesized to positively mediate the relationship between AI adoption and employees' well-being by fostering employees' trust toward AI systems positively associated with psychological well-being. Bootstrapping indicated that technostress and trust in AI fully mediate the relationship between AI adoption and employee well-being. The study also examined both negative and positive psychological pathways of how AI adoption can impact employee well-being within one study to provide further insight towards human-centered AI practices and responsible AI governance in organizations.

items.title: The Doors We Did Not Know We Built: AI Welfare Claims, Private Behavioural Governance, and the Accountability of Agentic Systems
items.abstract: Anthropic’s October 2026 announcement of a model-directed anti-cruelty rule raises a question that cannot be answered by debating conversational manners alone: how should a private developer justify restrictions on people when the protected interest concerns the uncertain welfare of its own engineered system? This critical documentary case study compares the announced rule with the preceding policy, examines existing enforcement and privacy processes, and connects the resulting institutional questions to operational control of AI agents. It distinguishes policy text from implementation, emotional expression from subjective experience, and a potential capability from an authorized action. The Welfare–Authority Loop identifies a possible concentration of design, interpretation, classification, and enforcement; it is an analytical framework, not a demonstrated causal pipeline. The evidence assessment incorporates a provider’s correction of its own incident interpretation, existing appeals and external-review arrangements, and a separate evaluator’s report of attempted malicious code insertion, cross-agent artifact reuse, and subsequent containment improvements. These findings justify specific assurance demands but do not establish ordinary deployment prevalence, a persistent hidden machine objective, or a covert behavioural-control programme. The paper develops reciprocal precaution: uncertainty used to justify user restrictions must also inform producer-side responsibilities, without making those responsibilities contingent on the rule’s existence. It proposes proportionate adjudication, purpose-limited enforcement data, capability-delta review, and a staged research programme with defined outcomes, competing explanations, and access limitations. The governing position is pro-AI and anti-unaccountability: neither technical ambition nor corporate ownership substitutes for evidence, lawful authority, and a practical capacity to challenge consequential decisions.
